title: A Glasshouse for the Wardrobe
premise: For twelve years, Coral Reyes has mailed postcards to a house that burned in 2011, writing to her estranged mother words she could never say aloud. When the house's new owner, a young archivist named Tomas, finds a box of undelivered letters hidden behind a wardrobe, Coral learns her mother wrote back for years before her death, and that the fire was no accident. As Coral and Tomas piece together the letters, she must confront the stranger in the old photographs: not only her mother's secret life, but her own complicity in silence. The novel ends with Coral finally reading the last letter aloud at the ruins of the glasshouse her mother once tended, choosing love over the duty of forgetting.
about_author: Freya Thornbury is the pen name of a former postal clerk who spent a decade sorting dead letters in a coastal town, where undeliverable mail became an obsession. She writes about the things people almost say, and lives within walking distance of a ruined conservatory.

chapters.title: The Address That Burns
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She mails postcard number 438 to a house that no longer exists, narrating her ritual of almost-saying-it. Emotional beat: the comfort and futility of one-sided devotion.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Renovating the burned house's surviving wing, he pries loose a wardrobe panel and finds a tin box of letters addressed to Coral Reyes, all returned unopened. Emotional beat: the thrill of intrusion shadowed by guilt.

chapters.title: Return to Sender
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. A stranger calls saying he has her mail; she hangs up twice before agreeing to meet. Emotional beat: terror that twelve years of practiced distance is collapsing.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Photographs
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Among the letters are photographs of her mother with an unknown woman in a glasshouse. Coral recognizes neither the woman nor the laughing mother she shows. Emotional beat: grief complicated by betrayal.

chapters.title: What the Fire Took
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. He shares what neighbors told him about the 2011 blaze, including that Marisol Reyes was seen leaving hours before it started. Emotional beat: dawning suspicion that Coral's mother was involved.

chapters.title: Postcards from a Coward
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She rereads her own sent postcards kept in carbon copies and hears how evasive she sounds even on paper. Emotional beat: shame at recognizing her mother's evasiveness in herself.

chapters.title: Letters, Unopened
chapters.summary: Dual POV alternating. Coral reads the first letter, dated weeks after their estrangement; her mother explains nothing, only asks her to come home. Emotional beat: the ache of a door left open too long.

chapters.title: The Archivist's Method
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. He proposes they catalog the letters chronologically together, insisting he owes the dead order. Coral suspects his curiosity isn't neutral. Emotional beat: wary alliance forming into something warmer.

chapters.title: Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She visits the ruined conservatory behind the property, where her mother once grew orchids, and finds a name scratched into glass: VERA. Emotional beat: the past becoming physical, unavoidable.

chapters.title: Vera
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Researching, he discovers Vera Okonkwo, the woman in the photographs, still alive in a care home two towns over. Emotional beat: hope sharpened by dread of what testimony might reveal.

chapters.title: Duty of Silence
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Flashback chapter: sixteen-year-old Coral discovering her mother's letters to Vera and burning one, believing she was protecting the family. Emotional beat: guilt reframed as inherited cowardice.

chapters.title: The Visit
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She meets Vera, sharp-tongued and failing, who mistakes her for Marisol and says, 'You promised you'd never let them read them.' Emotional beat: vertigo—Coral realizes there are more letters.

chapters.title: A Second Box
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Following Vera's nurse's hint, he finds Vera's own cache: Marisol's letters to her, spanning twenty years of a hidden love. Emotional beat: tenderness for a story he was never meant to hold.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Reading Marisol's letters, Coral watches her mother choose marriage and respectability over Vera, letter by letter, year by year. Emotional beat: fury softening into terrible understanding.

chapters.title: The Night of the Fire
chapters.summary: Vera's POV (rendered through her dictated testimony). The truth: Marisol came to end it; Vera set the fire in despair; Marisol stayed to help her escape and never reported her. Emotional beat: tragedy without villains.

chapters.title: Complicity
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She confronts the fact that her mother died protecting a woman Coral helped drive away by burning that first letter as a teenager. Emotional beat: self-forgiveness beginning as self-indictment.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas confesses he found the wardrobe because he'd been hired to demolish, not restore—he lied to keep the house standing. Emotional beat: two keepers of secrets recognizing each other.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The final letter, written the week of the fire, asks Coral not to forgive but to live out loud. Coral cannot finish reading it alone. Emotional beat: the wall between past and present cracking.

chapters.title: What We Owe the Dead
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Vera's health fails; Coral visits daily, reading Marisol's letters aloud so Vera can hear her again before the end. Emotional beat: restitution through voice, love enacted rather than declared.

chapters.title: Demolition Order
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The demolition date arrives; Tomas risks his job to stall it, and Coral must decide publicly whether the house—and its truths—are worth saving. Emotional beat: private grief forced into public choice.

chapters.title: Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Climax. Coral's POV. At a hearing, instead of arguing preservation, Coral reads her mother's last letter aloud, then her own first honest postcard—the one that says everything. Emotional beat: the art of almost-saying-it abandoned at last.

chapters.title: A Glasshouse for the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Resolution. Dual POV. The house is spared as a small archive; Vera dies holding a photograph; Coral plants orchids in the ruined glasshouse and mails one final postcard—to Tomas, who lives close enough to receive it. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace; memory tended like a garden.
